strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important gap: primate behavior recognition suffers from scarce labels and human-centric video pretraining. A 424-hour primate-centric pretraining corpus spanning web video plus research/observational data is a useful contribution for computer vision applied to ethology and conservation.

The experimental evidence is reasonably broad for this domain. The method is evaluated on four primate behavior datasets covering zoo, camera-trap, and drone settings, with both class-balanced and support-weighted metrics where appropriate.

The ablations support the main data-centric claims: curated YouTube data outperforms random YouTube data, R&O and YT-Filtered are both useful, combining them is best, and primate-centric cropping substantially improves validation performance.

The frozen-classifier setup is practical and attractive for low-label scientific datasets. The proposed narrow attentive head is simple, parameter-efficient, and often improves over much larger heads, which strengthens the usefulness of the approach beyond just pretraining another backbone.

The paper is mostly clear about dataset construction, pretraining recipe, downstream evaluation protocols, and limitations, including the limited diversity of evaluated species and the reliance on ground-truth boxes in downstream experiments.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The core model is V-JEPA with continual pretraining, plus a relatively straightforward attentive classifier; the main contribution is dataset curation and empirical validation rather than a new learning algorithm.

The strongest reported results still depend on ground-truth bounding boxes for downstream evaluation. This substantially simplifies the behavior-recognition task and leaves unclear how well the approach performs in an end-to-end deployment setting where detection/tracking errors compound.

Reproducibility is not fully resolved. The authors state that 14% of PriVi cannot be released, and the YouTube component depends on curated playlists and filtering decisions. This may make exact reproduction of pretraining results difficult even if code and most data are released.

The comparison to prior work is useful but uneven. Some baselines are taken from prior papers, some are reproduced, and coverage differs across datasets; there is limited discussion of whether all methods use the same crops, labels, splits, temporal context, and model-selection protocol.

There are no confidence intervals or statistical tests, despite small datasets, cross-validation in ChimpBehave, and multiple trained classifier heads. Several improvements are large enough to be convincing, but smaller differences, such as some CID or classifier-head gains, are harder to interpret.

The relevance classifier and detector used for dataset curation are only lightly validated. The relevance filter is trained from 2,500 images labeled by one annotator, and the impact of false positives/negatives, species imbalance, and potential web-data bias is not deeply analyzed.
The paper claims an Appendix for AlphaChimp protocol details, but the provided manuscript has no appendix. This weakens confidence in the reproducibility and fairness of that comparison.

There is a technical/presentation inconsistency in the V-JEPA loss notation: the text says masked tokens are predicted from unmasked tokens, but the equation appears to feed masked tokens to the context encoder and compare to the complement. This is likely a notation error but should be fixed for correctness and clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and under-served computer vision problem: primate behavior recognition in low-label, real-world settings. A primate-centric video pretraining dataset and evaluation across multiple primate benchmarks would be useful to the community if released as described.

The empirical story is coherent: PriVi improves over the original V-JEPA backbone on ChimpACT, PanAf500, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave, and the paper includes useful ablations for dataset composition, YouTube filtering, primate-centric cropping, in-domain continual pretraining, and classifier design.

The method is technically plausible and mostly simple: continual self-supervised V-JEPA pretraining plus a lightweight frozen attentive classifier. The simplicity makes the approach easier to understand and potentially easier to reuse than highly specialized architectures.

The data curation pipeline is a reasonable practical contribution, combining CLIP-based relevance filtering, cut detection, and zero-shot primate detection. The comparison between YT-Random and YT-Filtered supports the claim that curation matters.
The paper is generally clear, with enough architectural and training details to understand the main approach, and it reports both class-balanced and support-weighted metrics for the downstream tasks.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The core modeling recipe is largely an application of existing V-JEPA-style self-supervised pretraining and frozen attention heads to a domain-specific dataset; the main contribution is data curation and empirical validation, not a substantially new algorithmic idea.

The claim of a general-purpose primate video model is stronger than the evidence. Evaluation is limited to behavior classification on four datasets, mostly chimpanzees and baboons, and the authors acknowledge that experiments use ground-truth annotated bounding boxes. This does not yet demonstrate a general end-to-end video model for wild primate analysis, detection, tracking, or broader taxonomic generalization.

Reproducibility is weakened by partial dataset release: 14% of the pretraining data cannot be shared, and many source details are necessarily high-level. Since the principal contribution is data-centric, incomplete release and limited transparency about source overlap, licensing, and filtering decisions materially affect verifiability.

The baseline comparison is not fully satisfying. Table 4 contains sparse prior results across datasets, some baselines are only reported for one benchmark, and the paper relies partly on reproduced or protocol-incompatible comparisons. This makes the state-of-the-art claim less decisive than the text suggests.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates or statistical tests despite small datasets and five trained classifiers. Reporting means without variance makes it hard to assess whether smaller gains, such as some CID improvements, are robust.

The data curation labels are produced by one annotator and the relevance classifier is evaluated only on a held-out validation set from that labeling process. There is no analysis of annotation ambiguity, inter-annotator reliability, or failure modes of the detector/filtering pipeline, which matters for a dataset paper.

There is possible ambiguity around data leakage or domain overlap between PriVi/R&O sources and downstream benchmarks. The paper should explicitly document whether any downstream videos, locations, or near-duplicate clips are included in pretraining, especially because in-domain pretraining is separately evaluated.

Some claims are overstated relative to the results. For example, in-domain continual pretraining improves balanced metrics in some cases but can reduce other metrics, such as PanAf500 accuracy, yet the discussion presents it mostly as uniformly beneficial.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and under-served CV application: general-purpose primate behavior recognition in low-label regimes. The motivation is compelling, and the shift from single-dataset specialist models to domain-centric video pretraining is well aligned with practical needs in ethology and conservation.

PriVi is a substantial contribution: 424 hours of curated primate video from research/observational data and web video, with a clear curation pipeline using CLIP-based relevance filtering and zero-shot primate detection. The dataset composition and filtering choices are described in useful detail.

The empirical case is strong overall. The paper evaluates on four primate behavior datasets and reports consistent gains over a V-JEPA baseline, including improvements on PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave. Table 4 shows especially clear gains on ChimpACT mAP/mAPw and ChimpBehave accuracy/balanced accuracy.

The ablation study is unusually helpful for this kind of dataset/model paper. The authors separately test YT-Filtered, R&O, YT-Random, PriVi, in-domain continual pretraining, primate-centric cropping, and attentive classifier design choices, supporting the claim that both curation and architecture choices matter.

The frozen attentive classifier is a practical contribution: it is lightweight, appears less prone to overfitting than larger attentive heads, and is appropriate for small labeled animal behavior datasets.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and reproducible at a high level, with training compute, model scale, evaluation metrics, and dataset processing steps reported.
weaknesses: The main acceptance concern is evaluation scope relative to the breadth of the dataset claim. PriVi contains diverse primates and settings, but downstream evaluation is limited to chimpanzees/gorillas and baboons, and the paper itself notes that labeled evaluation datasets are limited. This weakens the evidence for a broadly general-purpose primate model.

All experiments rely on ground-truth bounding boxes at evaluation time, while many practical deployments would require detection/tracking plus behavior recognition. The paper acknowledges this, but it materially limits the demonstrated usefulness of the system as an end-to-end field tool.

The in-domain continual pretraining setup is not fully specified from a protocol perspective. It is unclear whether unlabeled target-domain pretraining uses only training-split videos or also validation/test videos. If the latter, the comparison to prior supervised methods becomes partly transductive and should be interpreted cautiously.

Reproducibility is good in outline but incomplete in important details. The paper states that code, models, and most of the dataset will be released, but 14% of PriVi cannot be released, and YouTube-sourced data may be difficult to reproduce exactly. More exact hyperparameters for V-JEPA pretraining and filtering thresholds would also help.

The state-of-the-art comparison is convincing in trend but somewhat uneven: several baselines report results only on subsets of benchmarks, and AlphaChimp requires the authors' own reproduction due to protocol mismatch. This is understandable, but it means the strongest comparative claims should be read with some care.

The paper reports averages over multiple classifier trainings but does not provide standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Given the small size and imbalance of some benchmarks, uncertainty estimates would strengthen the evidence.

Some claims could be more carefully worded. For example, 'surpasses the state of the art on all four datasets' is supported by the presented table under the selected protocols and metrics, but the heterogeneous baseline coverage and use of ground-truth boxes make the claim less absolute than the prose suggests.
